power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: There is limited research on persistent or recurrent depression into young adulthood.

We examined the prevalence of recurrent/persistent depression in young adults, and associations with childhood trauma/adversity and systemic inflammation, and if inflammatory markers mediated associations between childhood trauma and subsequent depression.

ALSPAC participants with ICD-10 depression assessments at ages 18, 24 and 30 were classified as never depressed, transiently depressed (one episode), or persistently/recurrently depressed (≥2 episodes).
Trauma/adversity from birth to age 16/17 was characterised by type, timing and burden.
Interleukin-6 (IL-6) and C-reactive protein (CRP) were measured at ages 9, 16, 18 and 24.
Analyses used multinomial logistic regression, linear regression and causal mediation models.
Among 2,014 participants, 78.9% were never depressed, 15.0% had transient depression and 6.1% had persistent/recurrent depression.

Trauma/adversity was more strongly associated with persistent/recurrent depression (RRR 3.17, 95% CI 1.98-5.06; FDR-P=6.2×10⁻⁶) than transient depression, with a dose-response pattern and stronger associations for threat adversities.
Middle-tolate childhood (11-17 yrs) emerged as a sensitive period for persistent/recurrent (RRR 2.85, 95% CI 1.47-5.52) and transient depression (RRR 1.85, 95% CI 1.25-2.73).
Trauma/adversity was associated with modestly higher IL-6 at age 24 (all FDR-adjusted P<0.05); CRP associations did not survive multipletesting correction.
text.formatted: Trauma/adversity was associated with modestly higher IL-6 at age 24 (all FDR-adjusted P<0.05); CRP associations did not survive multipletesting correction.

text.text: Neither marker mediated trauma/adversity associations with persistent/recurrent depression.
Persistent/recurrent depression affects approximately 1 in 20 young adults.
Childhood trauma/adversity, particularly during middle-to-late childhood, was associated with persistent/recurrent depression, but measured inflammatory proteins did not mediate this association.
Further work is needed to understand biological mechanisms underlying the embedding early life psychosocial stress.
Depression commonly emerges in early life and often follows a chronic, relapsing-remitting course.
Approximately 35% of mood disorders begin before age 25 (Solmi et al., 2022), with depression typically emerging earlier (Bromet et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Approximately 35% of mood disorders begin before age 25 <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Solmi et al., 2022)</ref>, with depression typically emerging earlier <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bromet et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Persistent, recurrent depression during adolescence to early adulthood imposes significant personal and clinical burden, including impaired social, educational, and occupational functioning (Thapar et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Persistent, recurrent depression during adolescence to early adulthood imposes significant personal and clinical burden, including impaired social, educational, and occupational functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Thapar et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, the prevalence of persistent/recurrent depression in young adults during the second and third decades of life remain poorly characterised.

It is also unclear how established psychosocial and biological risk factors, such as childhood trauma/adversity and inflammation (Mac Giollabhui et al., 2025; Nelson et al., 2017; Watson et al., 2025), for depression relate to persistent/recurrent depression into adulthood.
text.formatted: It is also unclear how established psychosocial and biological risk factors, such as childhood trauma/adversity and inflammation <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Mac Giollabhui et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Nelson et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Watson et al., 2025)</ref>, for depression relate to persistent/recurrent depression into adulthood.

text.text: Childhood trauma/adversity, often assessed using adverse childhood experience (ACE) measures (Felitti et al., 1998), has a strong, dose-response relationship with the risk and severity of depression throughout life (Flouri et al., 2020; Iob et al., 2022; LeMoult et al., 2020; Nanni et al., 2012; Tan & Mao, 2023).

text.text: Beyond cumulative exposure, the nature and developmental timing of adversity may influence subsequent depression.

Threat-related adversities have shown stronger associations with elevated depressive symptom trajectories than other ACEs (Iob et al., 2022) and maltreatment has been associated with a more persistent/recurrent course of depression with poorer treatment outcomes (Nanni et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Threat-related adversities have shown stronger associations with elevated depressive symptom trajectories than other ACEs <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Iob et al., 2022)</ref> and maltreatment has been associated with a more persistent/recurrent course of depression with poorer treatment outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Nanni et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: However, the extent to trauma/adversity type and timing are differentially associated with transient or persistent/recurrent depression into adulthood remains unclear.
Altered systemic inflammation may link ACEs with the development and persistence of depression.

A meta-analysis of longitudinal studies associated higher circulating interleukin-6 (IL-6) and C-reactive protein (CRP) concentrations with subsequent depressive symptoms, although associations were small (Mac Giollabhui et al., 2021).

text.text: In the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC), higher childhood IL-6 was associated with depression at age 18 (Khandaker et al., 2014), while higher IL-6 at age 9 was associated with persistent depressive symptoms between ages 10 and 19, but not adolescentonset symptoms (Khandaker et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC), higher childhood IL-6 was associated with depression at age 18 <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Khandaker et al., 2014)</ref>, while higher IL-6 at age 9 was associated with persistent depressive symptoms between ages 10 and 19, but not adolescentonset symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Khandaker et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that inflammation may precede depression and be particularly relevant to persistent symptoms, supporting investigation of its potential mediating role between ACEs and depression.
Evidence linking childhood trauma/adversity to systemic inflammation is mixed, with associations varying by adversity type, sex, inflammatory marker and age at assessment.

Lacey et al. reported that parental separation or divorce was associated with higher IL-6, whereas several other adversities were associated with lower IL-6, with further differences according to the sex of the child (Lacey et al., 2020). Crick et al. found no evidence of associations between cumulative or individual ACEs and inflammatory marker glycoprotein acetyls (GlycA) from ages 8 to 24, but observed a small association between cumulative ACE exposure and GlycA among mothers at age 49 (Crick et al., 2022).

text.text: Similarly, older adults reporting three or more ACEs retrospectively had chronically elevated CRP compared with those reporting none (Iob et al., 2020).

text.text: These findings suggest that inflammatory correlates of adversity may differ across the life course, although their biological significance remains uncertain.
Further investigation is therefore needed to establish whether adversity-related inflammation helps explain transient or persistent/recurrent depression across young adulthood.

Despite evidence linking childhood adversity to depression, and separate evidence implicating inflammation in depression risk and further separate evidence linking trauma/adversity to inflammatory disturbances, relatively little is known about how trauma exposure, inflammatory biomarkers, and depression course are related within the same longitudinal framework into early adulthood.
Inflammation may mediate the relationship between trauma/adversity and later depression, but current evidence is limited and focuses on IL-6 in childhood (up to age 10) (Flouri et al., 2020).

text.text: Repeated assessments extending into the third decade of life provide an opportunity to distinguish depression identified at a single assessment from depression present at multiple assessments, and to examine whether these patterns share early-life risk factors.
Understanding these associations could inform efforts to prevent enduring depression and clarify potential biological pathways linking childhood adversity with later mental health.

Using data from ALSPAC, a population-based prospective birth cohort, we have examined the longitudinal course of depression in young adults based on ICD-10 diagnosis of depression at ages 18, 24 and 30 years identifying those with transient (one episode) and persistent/recurrent (two or more episodes) depression.

We have examined the associations of transient and persistent/recurrent depression with: i) childhood trauma/adversity including the impact of specific trauma types, cumulative exposure, and developmental timing of trauma exposure; and ii) systemic inflammatory marker levels in blood from childhood through to adulthood including any mediating effects of inflammation on the trauma-depression relationship.
This study uses data from the ALSPAC cohort.
Pregnant women resident in Avon, UK with expected dates of delivery between 1st April 1991 and 31 st December 1992 were invited to take part in ALSPAC.
The initial number of pregnancies enrolled was 14,541.
Of these initial pregnancies, 13,988 children were alive at 1 year of age.
When the children were approximately 7 years old, an attempt was made to expand the initial sample by recruiting eligible participants who had not originally enrolled.
The total sample available for analyses using data collected after age 7 increased to 15,447 pregnancies, resulting in 15,658 foetuses.
Of these, 14,901 children were alive at 1 year of age (Boyd et al., 2013; Fraser et al., 2013; Northstone et al., 2019 Northstone et al., , 2026)).

Childhood trauma/adversity was assessed using two sets of variables available in ALSPAC: trauma variables and adverse childhood experience (ACE) variables.

Levels of CRP were measured in blood samples collected at ages 9, 16, 18 and 24 years, and IL-6 levels were measured in blood samples collected at ages 9 and 24 (see Supplementary Methods 1 for further information).
CRP concentrations (mg/L) were measured using ELISA and standardised to Z-scores prior to analysis.

text.text: Longitudinal depression groups were defined using ICD-10 depression diagnoses at ages 18, 24, and 30 years.

Participants were classified as never depressed (no diagnosis at any assessment), transiently depressed (a diagnosis at one assessment only), or persistently/recurrently depressed (a diagnosis at two or more assessments).
The main analysis included participants with depression status available at all three assessments and those whose longitudinal classification could be determined despite missing data.

Specifically, participants with depression at two assessments and missing status at the third were classified as persistently/recurrently depressed, as the missing value could not alter their classification (see Supplementary Methods 2).
ICD-10 depression diagnoses at ages 18, 24, and 30 years were also examined as separate binary outcomes, with participants classified as depressed or not depressed at each assessment.
Potential confounders included sex, ethnicity, maternal age at delivery, maternal education and maternal social class.
Biomarker analyses were additionally adjusted for blood collection variables (month of collection, time of collection and infection status).

text.text: Overall, childhood trauma/adversity was consistently associated with increased risk of subsequent depression, with stronger associations observed for persistent/recurrent depression than transient depression.

Individuals exposed to any childhood trauma/adversity had over three times the risk of persistent/recurrent depression compared with those reporting no trauma (RRR 3.17, 95% CI 1.98-5.06, FDR-P = 6.2 × 10⁻⁶), while the association with transient depression was more modest (RRR 1.65, 95% CI 1.26-2.16, FDR-P = 2.46 × 10⁻ 3 ).
Among individual trauma/adversity types, threat related types had the strongest associations with depression.

Physical cruelty (RRR 2.91, 95% CI 1.93-4.37, FDR-P = 2.25 × 10⁻⁶), sexual abuse (RRR 2.86, 95% CI 1.75-4.67, FDR-P = 9.07 × 10⁻ 5 ), physical abuse (RRR 2.45, 95% CI 1.53-3.92, FDR-P = 4.29 × 10⁻ 4 ) and emotional cruelty (RRR 2.37, 95% CI 1.55-3.59, FDR-P = 1.49 × 10⁻ 5 ) were all associated with a substantially increased risk of persistent/recurrent depression.

These associations were consistently stronger than those observed for transient depression, although sexual abuse, physical abuse and physical cruelty also remained significantly associated with transient depression.
Continuous measures of cumulative trauma/adversity (ACE score and trauma count) showed evidence of dose-response in their associations with depression.

Each additional reported trauma increased the risk of persistent/recurrent depression by 65% (RRR 1.65, 95% CI 1.43-1.91, FDR-P = 2.24 x 10⁻ 10 ), while each additional ACE score points increased risk by 44% (RRR 1.44, 95% CI 1.24-1.68, FDR-P = 6.2 x 10 -6 ).
Associations were also evident for transient depression, although effect sizes were consistently smaller.

Adjustment for sex, ethnicity, maternal age, maternal education, and maternal social class had little impact on the observed associations, with adjusted and unadjusted models yielding very similar results.

To investigate whether there is a sensitive period during which trauma is more strongly associated with subsequent depression, trauma exposure was examined across three developmental periods: 0-5, 5-11 and 11-17 yrs, using both binary and continuous measures (Figure 3, Supplementary Table 8).

text.text: Overall, trauma exposure during middle childhood (5-11 yrs) and adolescence (11-17 yrs) was associated with later depression, whereas there was little evidence of an association for exposure during early childhood (0-5 yrs).

Both any trauma exposure and trauma count during middle childhood (5-11 yrs) were associated with persistent/recurrent depression (RRR = 2.49, 95% CI 1.27-4.90, FDR-P = 0.0119; and RRR = 1.34, 95% CI 1.07-1.67, FDR-P = 0.0151, respectively), with little evidence of associations with transient depression.
Trauma exposure in late childhood/adolescence (11-17 yrs) emerged as the period most strongly associated with later depression.

Participants exposed to any trauma during this period had almost three times the risk of persistent/recurrent depression (RRR = 2.85, 95% CI 1.47-5.52, FDR-P = 0.00572), and nearly two-fold higher risk of the transient depression (RRR = 1.85, 95% CI 1.25-2.73, FDR-P = 0.00609), compared to the never depressed group.

Similarly, each additional traumatic event experienced between 11-17 yrs was associated with an 83% increase in the risk of persistent/recurrent depression (RRR = 1.83, 95% CI 1.45-2.32, FDR-P = 1.42 × 10⁻⁶) and a 46% increase in the risk of transient depression (RRR = 1.46, 95% CI 1.23-1.74, FDR-P = 5.8 × 10⁻ 6 ).

To determine whether these findings simply reflected the temporal proximity between trauma exposure (11-17 yrs) and depression measurement (the first CIS-R assessment was at 18 yrs), we next examined the associations between trauma experienced between 11-17 yrs and depression at ages 18, 24 and 30 yrs (Figure 4).

text.text: These results revealed that trauma occurring between 11-17 yrs had similar effects on depression at ages 18, 24 and 30 yrs.

Using the continuous trauma count measure, we found that with each additional traumatic event was associated with increased odds of depression at age 18 (OR = 1.59, 95% CI 1.30-1.94, FDR-P = 2.32 x 10 -6 ), age 24 (OR = 1.84, 95% CI 1.52-2.22, FDR-P =1.23 x 10 -9 ), and age 30 (OR = 1.26, 95% CI 1.02-1.56, FDR-P = 4.64 x 10 -2 ).

These findings suggest that the stronger associations observed for trauma during adolescence are unlikely to be explained solely by the temporal proximity of trauma exposure to the first depression assessment.
Childhood adversity/trauma was associated with higher IL-6 concentrations at age 24 after adjustment for potential confounders, although effect sizes were generally modest.

Associations were observed for ACE score (β = 0.027, 95% CI 0.002-0.052, FDR-P = 0.036), trauma count (β = 0.050, 95% CI 0.025-0.076, FDR-P = 4.55 × 10⁻⁴), and any trauma (β = 0.100, 95% CI 0.040-0.160, FDR-P = 0.002) (see Figure 5, Supplementary Table 9).

Associations were observed for trauma count during both periods (5-11 years: β = 0.061, 95% CI 0.026-0.096, FDR-P = 7.24 × 10⁻⁴; 11-17 years: β = 0.076, 95% CI 0.033-0.118, FDR-P = 7.25 × 10⁻⁴) and for any trauma (5-11 years: β = 0.093, 95% CI 0.032-0.155, FDR-P = 0.004; 11-17 years: β = 0.108, 95% CI 0.046-0.171, FDR-P = 0.002).
Results were similar across models adjusting for biomarker collection covariates and sociodemographic characteristics.
There was little evidence that trauma exposure during early childhood (0-5 yrs), assessed as either trauma count or any trauma, was associated with IL-6 at age 24.
Associations between trauma exposure and CRP at age 24 did not survive correction for multiple testing (see Supplementary Table 9 and Supplementary Results).

Persistent or recurrent depression affects approximately 1 in 20 young adults across ages 18, 24 and 30 years.
Our findings showed that childhood trauma was consistently associated with depression in young adulthood, with stronger associations for persistent/recurrent depression than for transient depression.

Threat-related adversities showed the strongest association with persistent/recurrent depression, and cumulative trauma showed a clear dose-response relationship, suggesting that both the type and burden of childhood adversity are important risk factors for depression into adulthood.

Although trauma was associated with higher systemic inflammatory marker levels in later childhood (11-17 yrs), these did not appear to be a major explanatory pathway linking trauma exposure to depression.
Incorporating newly available age-30 depression assessments allowed us to extend the study of depression course beyond early adulthood.
Extensive evidence links childhood trauma/adversity with later depression (Flouri et al., 2020; Iob et al., 2022; LeMoult et al., 2020; Nanni et al., 2012; Tan & Mao, 2023).

text.text: We therefore examined whether the adolescent association reflected proximity to the first depression assessment at age 18.

Trauma between 11-17 yrs was associated with depression at ages 18 and 24, and trauma count remained associated with depression at age 30, suggesting longer-term relevance beyond proximity to the first outcome assessment, although associations did weaken over time.
Notably, a similar timing pattern was observed for inflammation, with trauma exposure in mid to late childhood also showing stronger associations with IL-6 at age 24.
Associations between childhood trauma/adversity and CRP were largely attenuated to the null, consistent with findings from previous studies (Crick et al., 2022; Flouri et al., 2020).

text.text: Our work highlights that trauma exposure, particularly threat-related adversity and cumulative trauma burden, may be more strongly associated with recurrent patterns of depression than with isolated depressive episodes.

The strong associations observed for threat-related adversities are in line with dimensional models of childhood adversity, particularly the threat-deprivation framework proposed by McLaughlin and colleagues, which suggests that experiences involving threat, such as physical, sexual, or emotional abuse, may be especially relevant to socioemotional processing and later psychopathology (McLaughlin et al., 2014; Sheridan & McLaughlin, 2014).

text.text: Identifying trauma types that are more strongly associated with later mental health may help inform more targeted approaches to prevention and intervention.

Our work adds to existing reports showing that while childhood trauma is associated with higher levels of systemic inflammatory markers such as IL-6 and CRP, these do not fully mediate the traumadepression relationship (Flouri et al., 2020; Iob et al., 2022).

text.text: There are several possible explanations for this finding.
Raised inflammatory markers do not reflect/capture the aspect of immune response "shaped" or "programmed" by experiencing adversity/trauma.
It is also possible that raised inflammatory marker levels are not key mediating pathway linking trauma to depression, but other mechanisms are involved.
Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis functioning, which regulates cortisol and stress responsivity (Herman et al., 2016), has been suggested as a possible mediator.

text.text: Childhood adversity has been proposed to increase depression risk through allostatic overload of the HPA axis (Wilkinson & Goodyer, 2011), and broader evidence suggests that early adversity can become biologically embedded through interacting changes in stress physiology, immune function, neural development, and epigenetic regulation (Takahashi & Shelton, 2025; Vargovic et al., 2026; Zhou & Ryan, 2023).

text.text: These processes are highly relevant to depression, as dysregulated cortisol signalling, altered immune activity, and stress sensitisation may increase vulnerability to low mood, anhedonia, fatigue, cognitive symptoms, and impaired emotion regulation (Rousson et al., 2020).

text.text: Over time, such biological changes may lower resilience to later stressors, helping to explain why childhood trauma had greater association with persistent/recurrent depression than with transient depression.

Therefore, the absence of IL-6/CRP mediation in the present study does not rule out biological mechanisms but suggests that a single circulating inflammatory marker may be insufficient to capture the relevant pathways.
Strengths of this study includes the use of ALSPAC, a rich longitudinal cohort spanning childhood, adolescence, and young adulthood.

The inclusion of newly available CIS-R data at age 30 allowed depression trajectories to be extended beyond early adulthood, distinguishing persistent/recurrent from transient depression over a longer period than previous ALSPAC studies.
The detailed characterisation of childhood adversity allowed examination of cumulative trauma burden, specific trauma types, and developmental timing.
The availability of inflammatory biomarker data across childhood allowed trauma-related differences in systemic inflammation to be assessed across development.

Multiple imputation, incorporating a range of auxiliary variables, was used to reduce bias from missing data; imputed findings were broadly consistent with complete-case sensitivity analyses, although completecase estimates were less precise.
Limitations include attrition over time, limited geographic and ethnic diversity, and potential biases arising from self-reported or parent-reported data.

Notably, trauma exposure was higher among participants with missing depression repeat assessment data than among those in either observed depression group, suggesting that attrition may have led to underestimation, rather than overestimation, of the association between childhood trauma and later depression.
Prospective assessment of childhood adversity is a key strength.
However, most ALSPAC adversity measures before age 8 were parent-reported.
Although both parent-and child-reported trauma predict later mental health outcomes (Croft et al., 2019), caregivers may underreport maltreatment (Dunn et al., 2026).

text.text: While reporting source may have introduced measurement error, the observed associations are unlikely to be entirely attributable to one informant type.
Possible underreporting, particularly in early childhood, may have led to exposure misclassification and attenuation of associations with later depression.
In conclusion, our study shows the extent of persistent or recurrent depression between late adolescence and young adulthood between ages 18 and 30 years, which affect approx. 1 in 20 individuals.
It also identifies abuse/maltreatment, especially threat adversities experienced during middle and late childhood as potentially important risk factors for persistent depression in young adults.
This work also highlights research gaps by highlighting the need for identifying biological mechanisms linking early-life adversity and adult depression.
